issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette: Ravi, a 41-year-old South Asian graphic designer, has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic encounter with police during which he experienced profound fear and distress. The event occurred about six months ago when he was wrongfully detained by the local police department after being mistakenly identified as a suspect in an unrelated crime. Ravi had come to believe that the world is inherently dangerous, and that people cannot be trusted. This belief has permeated his daily life, affecting both his personal relationships and professional environment. His occupation as a graphic designer has made him acutely aware of authority figures; every interaction with uniformed personnel or even discussions about future projects now triggers intense anxiety. The incident began when he was leaving work one evening. As he approached his car in the parking lot, he noticed several police cars and officers on patrol nearby. The smell of burning rubber and smoke from a recent fire at another part of the complex triggered an immediate flood of memories. Ravi had been certain that this was the same scent he smelled during his wrongful detention, which made him feel like he was reliving the traumatic event all over again. He vividly recalls being led into the station and questioned for hours while officers in full uniform surrounded him. The memory is still so vivid that it feels as though it happened just yesterday. Each time Ravi tries to recount what occurred, he finds himself unable to express his experience clearly. He knows what transpired but struggles to find the words or even loses the thread of his narrative mid-sentence. To cope with these intense feelings, Ravi has started rehearsing conversations before any interaction, a maladaptive strategy that has led him to become increasingly isolated from his colleagues and friends. Making plans for the future is now nearly impossible; he avoids scheduling events or making commitments out of fear that something similar might happen again. Ravi's hypervigilance towards people has also taken a toll on his work. He is constantly scanning his surroundings, looking for signs of danger or suspicious behavior. This constant vigilance has made it difficult to focus on his projects and deadlines, leading to increased stress and tension at the office. His wife has noticed these changes in him as well; he avoids going out together and often cancels plans at the last minute. The guilt he feels when recalling the event is overwhelming; he believes that if he had done something differently or been more cautious, none of this would have happened. His inability to articulate his feelings clearly further exacerbates his distress. It was these mounting difficulties in both his personal life and work that finally compelled Ravi to seek help. He was certain that the only way to reclaim control over his life was through therapy. What frightens him most is not just the possibility of another traumatic encounter, but the loss of the relationships and career he values so deeply. Ravi hopes for a future where he can trust others again and feel safe in his surroundings without constantly monitoring his environment or avoiding interactions out of fear. He believes that with proper support, he can regain his sense of security and move forward from this traumatic experience.
